title: War: Watt Is It Good For?
gist: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich argue that modern warfare — drones, AI-enabled autonomy, and offensive cyber — is converging on a single 'electrotech' stack (batteries, motors, power electronics, embedded compute) that China dominates industrially even as it democratizes battlefield capability, and that Washington is undermining its own response by gutting the civilian EV/battery demand base (post-IRA-repeal) that the Pentagon now needs as an industrial reserve, proposing a battery-tech alliance between defense hawks and clean-energy advocates as the fix.

insights.claim: A single technology stack the authors call 'electrotech' — the integrated hardware/software that generates, stores, and directs electricity — now underlies drones, electric vehicles, AI compute, and offensive cyber capabilities simultaneously, meaning a battlefield increasingly runs on the same batteries, motors, and embedded compute as consumer electric vehicles and smartphones.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Investors in defense tech should treat battery/power-electronics supply chains as a direct proxy for military capability, not a separate 'clean energy' vertical — capacity in one (EVs, grid storage) directly fungible into the other (drones, AI data centers).

insights.claim: Cheap, battery-powered drones built largely on consumer foundations are now responsible for the overwhelming majority of casualties in the war in Ukraine, while unmanned hybrid-electric ground vehicles are beginning to displace infantry there.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Confirms battery-powered unmanned systems have already become the dominant lethality driver on a major modern battlefield — a strong demand signal for battery, motor, and embedded-compute suppliers to the defense sector.
insights.locator: The Electrotech Transformation of the Battlefield

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone pilots facing Russian radiofrequency jamming are developing platforms with enough onboard AI to find and strike targets independently of remote piloting, and the lightweight open-source AI tools running this autonomy are free but the electricity ('watts') to power them is not — greater autonomy requires more onboard battery storage.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Identifies battery energy density, not AI software, as the binding constraint on further battlefield-autonomy gains — a specific hardware bottleneck to watch for investment and R&D breakthroughs.
insights.quote: the watts to run them are not [free]
insights.locator: This transformation looks like a great democratization

insights.claim: Anduril is bringing battery-powered, increasingly intelligent systems to higher-end defense segments, including 'unmanned wingmen' adapted from electric air taxi technology and modularized unmanned submarines.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Names Anduril as a company directly translating consumer/urban-mobility electric propulsion tech (air taxis) into defense products — a concrete example of the electrotech dual-use thesis in action.
insights.locator: The Electrotech Transformation of the Battlefield

themes.theme: China's industrial consolidation of the electrotech stack

insights.claim: Because consumer electronics, EVs, drones, and robots share the same industrial heritage (chips, materials science, supply chains, code), Chinese manufacturers like smartphone maker Xiaomi and battery maker BYD were able to become EV, drone, and robot companies easily, letting an advantage in any one sector propagate across all of them and creating self-sustaining investment flywheels.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Explains the structural mechanism behind China's cross-sector electrotech dominance — an investment thesis for why Chinese firms with consumer-electronics/EV heritage (like BYD, Xiaomi) can credibly expand into defense-adjacent autonomous systems markets.

insights.claim: Chinese President Xi Jinping elevated 'intelligentization' into official Chinese military doctrine in 2020, and China's military has since demonstrated its Atlas drone swarm system and is training unmanned naval attack platforms with Russia in joint exercises, preparing for a drone-saturated war over Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A dated (2020) doctrinal marker plus named hardware (Atlas drone swarm) demonstrating China's electrotech-military doctrine is mature and actively rehearsing a Taiwan contingency with Russia — relevant to Taiwan Strait conflict-risk timelines.

insights.claim: In response to Ukraine's lessons and China's electrotech industrial advantage, U.S. defense leaders are developing their first serious battery strategy and have requested $54 billion for a crash drone production program, while private capital has bestowed multibillion-dollar valuations on defense startups Anduril, Saronic, and Joby, all built on consumer-electronics-derived foundations.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A concrete budget figure ($54B crash drone program request) and named startup cohort (Anduril, Saronic, Joby) receiving multibillion-dollar valuations — direct signal of where U.S. defense-tech capital is currently concentrating.

insights.claim: China is adding whole countries' worth of electricity generation to its grid every year using authoritarian resolve to marshal watts, while the United States is stuck in a cycle of permitting hearings, and Chinese chipmakers are investing in large-scale chip orchestration on the bet that chips ten times less efficient paired with ten times more electricity can still narrow the compute gap with the U.S.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A specific counter-argument to the assumption that superior U.S. chip efficiency guarantees a lasting compute-capability edge — China's grid-scale electricity buildout could functionally offset a per-chip efficiency deficit, a risk factor for U.S. AI-compute-superiority theses.
insights.locator: Turning Watts into Weapons, and Pointing Weapons at Watts

themes.theme: Washington's self-sabotage: the IRA repeal and industrial reserve logic

insights.claim: The Inflation Reduction Act's electrotech industrial strategy — aiming to produce the batteries, motors, and software-hardware fusion the Pentagon now requires — was politically fatal because it was enacted under the banner of climate change; battery manufacturing incentives narrowly survived a partial repeal, but consumer EV incentives were zeroed out, gutting the demand growth those battery factories were built against.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Direct policy read-through: U.S. battery manufacturing capacity built for consumer EV demand now faces a demand shortfall after EV tax credit repeal, creating both a near-term overcapacity/utilization risk for battery plants and a defense-readiness gap the authors say the Pentagon can't fill alone.

insights.claim: The authors draw a direct historical analogy: Detroit automakers' midcentury tooling and engineering culture, built by selling generations of cars to families first, became the WWII 'Arsenal of Democracy' — implying that today's battery/motor/EV industrial reserve can only serve military needs if it is first built at civilian consumer scale.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Provides an explicit historical framework arguing that reviving consumer-scale EV/battery demand (not just defense procurement) is a prerequisite for defense-industrial surge capacity — relevant to how investors should read future EV/battery tax-credit debates as defense-relevant, not purely climate-relevant, policy.

insights.claim: The Pentagon now advocates for broader latitude to license foreign (Chinese) battery technologies and for tax incentives 'remarkably similar' to the Inflation Reduction Act's, revealing that the real obstacles to a new American 'arsenal of electricity' are cultural rather than technical, financial, or geopolitical.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Signals the Pentagon itself may push for IRA-like battery tax incentives to be reintroduced under a defense rather than climate framing — a policy reversal worth watching for battery-sector investors.
insights.locator: The Pentagon now advocates for broader latitude

insights.claim: The CHIPS and Science Act has proven far more durable as industrial policy than the IRA because its passing coalition was broad, anchored in geopolitical anxiety over Chinese chip dependency rather than climate goals — Trump regularly criticizes the bill but its implementation continues largely unencumbered by culture-war attacks.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A political-durability case study: industrial policy framed around China-competition/national-security survives partisan swings better than policy framed around climate goals — a template the authors argue electrotech/battery policy should adopt.
insights.locator: The CHIPS and Science Act stands in marked contrast

insights.claim: The authors propose that renewed EV tax credits won't be politically palatable soon, but all-purpose battery credits — covering cars, home backup, or even kitchen appliances — could rebuild the industrial reserve the Pentagon needs while anchoring allied industrial interoperability.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A specific, more politically viable policy alternative (application-agnostic battery credits vs. EV-specific credits) to watch for in future U.S. industrial-policy legislation.
insights.locator: An Unlikely Alliance for an Arsenal of Electricity

themes.theme: AI, cyber, and the electrified grid as a target

insights.claim: In April 2026, Anthropic's Mythos model kicked off a class of AI tools capable of autonomously discovering and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities, and the more electricity ('wattage') such models spend on vulnerability discovery, the more vulnerabilities they find — directly linking offensive/defensive cyber capability to raw electricity availability.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Establishes electricity supply as a direct input to cyber-offense capability via AI vulnerability-discovery tools (citing Anthropic's Mythos model) — a grid-capacity constraint that now has national-security cyber implications, not just AI-training implications.
insights.locator: Turning Watts into Weapons, and Pointing Weapons at Watts

insights.claim: American chips convert electricity into AI 'tokens' far more efficiently than Chinese chips, helping U.S. companies account for roughly 80 percent of global compute capacity — a margin the authors say comforts Pentagon cyber planners worried about being outnumbered by Chinese operators.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A concrete market-share figure (80% of global compute capacity held by U.S. companies) quantifying the current U.S. AI-compute lead, useful as a baseline to track for erosion given China's electricity-volume counter-strategy described elsewhere in the piece.
insights.locator: Luckily, American chips convert electricity into tokens

insights.claim: Beijing has spent years pre-positioning destructive cyber capabilities within the fragmented, aging U.S. electricity grid infrastructure in preparation for a potential war over Taiwan — a campaign the authors say predates the AI boom and the broader industrial electrification now straining the grid.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A specific, standing national-security threat (pre-positioned Chinese cyber capabilities in the U.S. grid) that grows more consequential as more of the economy and military capability becomes electricity-dependent — relevant to grid cybersecurity investment and utility-sector risk assessment.
insights.locator: That consolidation will also make energy infrastructure our adversaries' highest-value target

themes.theme: A framework for managing China component risk

insights.claim: The authors argue technical risk from Chinese components does not reside uniformly in any 'Made in China' sticker but should be prioritized by a 'smart-to-dumb' framework: raw-material dependencies (like graphite or wire) are slower-moving economic risks amenable to stockpiling, while digitally active control layers — software governing battery systems or navigation computers — pose the urgent risk of crippling cyberattacks in a conflict's opening hours.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Offers investors and policymakers a concrete triage framework for Chinese-component defense-supply-chain risk: prioritize scrutiny of embedded software/control systems over raw material inputs, rather than pursuing blanket component bans.

insights.claim: The authors note even the F-35 is not free of Chinese-made parts, and blanket bans on foreign components have long been ruled both unworkable and unnecessary by the defense industrial base.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: Undercuts blanket 'zero Chinese content' procurement proposals as impractical even for flagship platforms like the F-35 — relevant context for evaluating the feasibility of proposed China-decoupling defense procurement rules.
insights.locator: The defense industrial base already has the intuition

insights.claim: The authors' central policy recommendation is an alliance between the defense-tech and climate-tech communities: the defense ecosystem offers climate tech the political durability it has long sought, while clean energy offers the defense industrial base the entrepreneurial energy and consumer-market scale it has spent decades lacking.
insights.speaker: Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable coalition-building thesis: investors and policymakers should expect (and can help engineer) convergence between climate-tech/battery startups and defense primes as the path to durable U.S. electrotech industrial policy.
insights.locator: But each community holds precisely what the other lacks
